messages:
Marta: Ran a set of apples-to-apples runs this morning comparing synthetic client (wrk2-style) vs our replay harness against the kernel-selection+batcher change. Found a nasty tail when clients aren't reusing connections (HTTP keepalive off).
Dan: ugh, that pattern keeps biting us. numbers?
Marta: quick paste: perf-bot posted raw: p50=45ms p95=120ms p99=380ms with keepalive ON; p50=48ms p95=320ms p99=1.2s with keepalive OFF (same server binary). throughput ~flat but tails explode.
perf-bot: summary (same-run):
- mode: replay-harness
- kernel-selector: v2
- batching: dynamic, max_batch=64
- KV cache: enabled, prefix hit rate ~82%
- keepalive: true -> p99=380ms; keepalive:false -> p99=1.2s
Kian: do we see TLS handshake timeouts? probably the extra TLS + tcp handshake on every request. any difference between gRPC and rest?
Marta: yes. gRPC long-lived streams (grpc with HTTP2 keepalive) behaves well. HTTP/1.1 w/ new connection shows TLS+Nagle+slow-start cost. I ran a minimal repro with curl in a loop: 
```
for i in $(seq 1 1000); do curl -s -o /dev/null https://redwood.internal:443/char -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"prompt":"hi"}'; done
```
with keepalive disabled it takes ~2.1x longer overall and has 3-4x more requests hitting >500ms.
Olivia: did you try SO_REUSEPORT or connection pooling from the client harness? sometimes the synthetic harness opens many short-lived sockets causing transient CPU spikes in accept() path.
Marta: yes we tried REUSEPORT and bumping accept queue. REUSEPORT smoothed some variance but p99 still bad when keepalive off. The interesting bit: kernel selector makes different kernel choices depending on observed seq-len distribution. With more churn the runtime falls back to smaller-kernel path that is slightly cheaper per-token but much worse for cold-start latency (code-gen vs JIT path).
Dan: so client behavior changes which kernel is picked -> surprising. That explains mismatch between synthetic and replay.
Kian: can you share the flamegraph? I'm betting on a) TLS handshake, b) accept()/epoll_wait churn, c) batcher waiting due to jittered arrivals.
Marta: pasted a tiny excerpt from perf/0.svg text dump: 
```
40%   runtime::accept_loop
18%   ssl::do_handshake
12%   batcher::coalesce_or_flush
8%    kernel_selector::choose_small_kernel
5%    kv_cache::lookup
```
That accept loop + handshake dominates tails when keepalive disabled.
Olivia: Did you try tcp_nodelay (disable Nagle)? that'll reduce extra delays for small packets but increases packet overhead. Worth testing for small prompt sizes.
Marta: tested toggling TCP_NODELAY client-side: slight p50 improvement for tiny prompts but p99 still handshake-dominated. Also tried session resumption (TLS session ticket) — that helps a lot for repeated short lived connections if the client supports it.
Dan: What about gRPC unary vs streaming? For test parity we should compare (a) HTTP/1.1 new conn, (b) HTTP/1.1 keepalive, (c) gRPC unary (new conn), (d) gRPC with a long-lived bidi.
Marta: did that matrix. Results: streaming gRPC is best for tails, HTTP/1.1 keepalive ok, new-conn variants are worst. grpc unary with new conn still pays TLS + new TCP.
Kian: For apples-to-apples we need to standardize the client harness: keep persistent connections *or* instrument the runtime to include handshake cost in latency buckets explicitly. Right now our runtime reports only server processing time which hides client-side transport cost.
Marta: agreed. Also found the replay harness by default replays inter-arrival timestamps which in theory is closer to prod, but our synthetic harness bursts in micro-batches which nudges kernel selector to pick a different kernel. So both arrival pattern and connection behavior matter.
Olivia: action items?
Dan: list: 1) Make client harness config explicit about connection reuse and TLS session resumption. 2) Add an end-to-end latency metric (server processing + transport handshake) in the harness. 3) Add a 'cold-conn' testbed to capture worst-case p99. 4) Make kernel selector emit reason codes (why it picked small kernel). 5) Document guidance for customers: prefer connection pooling or grpc streaming for low tails.
Marta: did a quick PR for (1) and (2) on bench-runner. Example config snippet we added: 
```
client:
  keepalive: true
  tls_session_resumption: true
  reuse_port: false
  open_rate: 50/s
```
Dan: nice. Also let's capture tcp_info stats per request (rtt, retransmits) so we can correlate network jitter with batcher flush behavior.
Kian: one more gotcha: Nagle + TLS sometimes defers the first data packet until a small amount of data buffers up; combined with delayed ACKs on the client it can add ~40-200ms. For tiny-prompt workloads toggle NODELAY in the harness.
Marta: yep noted. Final note: perf regression we saw last week for kernel-selector v2 wasn't actually a runtime kernel bug — it was a test harness change (we disabled keepalive in a new synthetic config). Once we re-run with keepalive enabled the regression disappears. Moral: client-side benchmarking pitfalls can masquerade as server regressions. :facepalm:
